title: Dutch AI extension listing
description: One file per listing in data/listings/, named <id>.json. Every field is required; no optional fields.

id.description: Stable slug, and the filename. Join key for every surface and later usage events.

description_en.description: One outcome-first sentence. At most 200 characters: the cards that quote it clamp at three lines.

description_nl.description: Dutch mirror of description_en: one outcome-first sentence, same register, at most 200 characters. Product/vendor names stay untranslated.

subject.description: Keys from data/subjects.json of the Dutch service, data source, standard, or authority this integration lets an agent reach or work with; the outcome axis listings are grouped and searched by.

contains.$comment: All four arrays empty is what the old `bundles` meant by a one-artifact listing; under the self-listing rule it means a listing that gives you nothing, which is never a real submission — and it is the shape that makes the derived kind fall through to `bundle`.
contains.description: Everything the listing gives you, each kind in its own array, so the capabilities inside a single row stay findable. All four arrays are required and at least one carries a name — a listing that holds nothing is not a listing. Empty means none of that kind. A listing lists itself: a lone MCP server carries its own server name under `mcp_servers`, a lone skill its own name under `skills`. Names follow the publisher, falling back to the listing's `id` where the publisher ships no name. For a large multi-jurisdiction bundle, list only the Dutch-relevant entries. What kind of thing a listing is is read off these arrays — one kind is that kind, several is a bundle — rather than stored a second time.

skills.description: Skill names as the publisher ships them — the directory holding each SKILL.md. Shared-resource pseudo-skills (`_shared`) are infrastructure, not capabilities; leave them out.

commands.description: Slash-command names without the leading slash — the basename of each file in `commands/`.

agents.description: Subagent names — the basename of each file in `agents/`.

mcp_servers.description: Keys from the `mcpServers` config that serve the listing's purpose, including the listing's own server where the listing is one. The publisher's own ops plumbing (monitoring, admin backends) is not a capability; leave it out.

execution.description: Where the code has to execute: `local` is a process on the visitor's own machine (stdio — `npx`, `uvx`, `docker run`), `remote` is an HTTPS server the publisher already runs, `both` is the same server offered either way, `none` is a listing that runs nothing, such as instructions you copy in. A server that merely *supports* an HTTP transport is still `local` — what makes a listing `remote` is that a URL exists to paste, not that one could be made to exist. It decides whether a listing can be used at all: products that register a server from their own cloud cannot spawn a local process, so a `local` listing is unreachable there whatever the visitor does. A listing whose parts disagree takes the value of its most restrictive part — any local-only server in a bundle makes the listing `local`. Read it off the source; it follows neither the host nor `contains`. `none` means nothing executes, never that nobody checked, which is why a listing carrying an `mcp_servers` entry may not claim it.
execution.$comment: Spelled out rather than left blank: an empty string would read as unverified in the one field where that confusion is most expensive.

uses.description: Every external party the listing reaches, one entry per registrable domain, empty where it reaches none. Each entry says whether an account there stands between the visitor and the listing — a row rather than a bare list of required accounts, so the record can also say that a listing reaches an open service freely, which is roughly half the catalogue.

domain.description: The registrable domain of the party — never the portal subdomain that happens to issue the key: NS hands out keys at apiportal.ns.nl and the value here is `ns.nl`. Where a service runs a separate country domain, name the one a Dutch visitor signs in to (`exactonline.nl`). Nothing but this rule enforces the grain, since a pattern cannot know which label is registrable.

account.description: Whether the visitor must already hold an account here before the listing does anything. `false` is the informative direction and covers about half the catalogue — RDW, CBS, wetten.nl, KNMI and the rest of the open half. It records that an account stands in the way, not what it costs: a free self-serve developer key and a paid subscription are the same `true`, because price is a fact about the service and is not stored per listing. Not derivable from `subject` — one Rijksmuseum listing needs a key and another needs nothing, because it queries its own copy.

status.description: How far along the listing is, read off the source by the ladder in CONTRIBUTING.md. `live`, `beta`, `preview` and `concept` are a maturity ladder and every value on it but `live` comes from the publisher's own words — a README calling it beta, an *Alpha* heading, a disclaimer — because nothing here infers maturity from a version digit any more than from stars or age. `abandoned` and `broken` are off that ladder and are conditions we observed: `abandoned` needs the publisher to say so, and `broken` means the documented install does not run while another route does. So a status other than `live` always means either the publisher said it or somebody checked it, never that we guessed.
status.$comment: `broken` is appended rather than slotted in so the enum order still reads as the ladder followed by the two terminal conditions.

allOf.$comment: A listing that carries an MCP server executes something, so it cannot claim nothing does. This is what keeps a source nobody managed to read from being filed as `none` instead of being read.
